payload.name: modulation-spectrum
payload.scope: A computational analysis method that decomposes a time-frequency representation into slow and fast components, extracting temporal envelope structure of spectral content.

definition.body: Modulation spectrum is a signal analysis method that extracts the temporal envelope (amplitude modulation) structure of a time-frequency representation by computing a short-time Fourier transform along the frequency or time axis of a spectrogram. The procedure: (1) compute a spectrogram S(t,f); (2) choose a dimension (time or frequency) and compute the magnitude spectrum of S(t,f) along that dimension for each frame; (3) the result is a two-dimensional representation with frame rate and modulation rate axes. Parameters: the spectrogram frame rate, the FFT size along the modulation axis, the choice of axis, and the modulation rate range. Persistence: implemented in audio analysis libraries and speech processing toolkits, stored as a two-dimensional magnitude matrix. e.g.: modulation spectrogram in Kaldi's speech features module for phoneme-rate analysis; librosa's modulation spectrum for beat tracking at 2-20 Hz; the modulation features used in the TIMIT phoneme recognition baseline [formal: modulatio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: spectral-residual
payload.scope: The residual component remaining after smoothing a spectrogram, capturing the non-stationary and impulsive spectral content that the smooth envelope misses.

definition.body: Spectral residual is the difference between a log-power spectrogram and a smoothed estimate of its long-term average, computed by low-pass filtering the spectrogram along the time axis and subtracting the result. The procedure: (1) compute the log-power spectrogram log|S(t,f)|; (2) apply a temporal low-pass filter or moving average to obtain the smoothed estimate L(t,f); (3) subtract: R(t,f) = log|S(t,f)| - L(t,f). The result isolates the impulsive, transient, and non-stationary spectral content — peaks that stand out above the long-term spectral envelope. This residual is the basis of spectral peak detection algorithms, used in pitch tracking, speech enhancement, and source separation. Parameters: the spectrogram frame rate, the smoothing window length along time, and the normalization method. Persistence: implemented as a matrix in speech and audio analysis libraries, stored as a float array. e.g.: the spectral residual computed in the HTS-SPICE speech enhancement toolkit for noise robustness; the residual used in the HTS voice conversion pipeline to preserve speaker identity; the spectral peaks extracted from the residual in the HTS-HMM system for phoneme recognition [formal: residualis spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: interaural-time-difference
payload.scope: A binaural spatialization cue representing the inter-ear time delay used to encode sound direction in computational audio processing.

definition.body: Interaural-time-difference is a computational parameter used in binaural audio rendering that encodes the time delay between sound arrival at two ears, computed from a virtual source position relative to a head model. The procedure: (1) given a source direction (azimuth, elevation), compute the path length difference from the source to each ear using a head shape model (sphere or KEMAR head model); (2) convert the path difference to a time delay: ITD = delta_distance / speed_of_sound; (3) implement the delay using a digital delay line (fractional sample delay via interpolation). The ITD varies sinusoidally with azimuth (zero at 0 degrees, maximum ~0.63 ms at 90 degrees), encoding horizontal position. Combined with interaural level difference (ILD), it is a primary cue for binaural spatialization. Parameters: the virtual source position, the head radius (typically 0.0875 m for KEMAR), the maximum ITD, and the delay filter length. Persistence: implemented in binaural rendering engines (SOFA format HRTF processing, Ambisonic toolkits), stored as a parameter in spatial audio standards. e.g.: the ITD computed in the ITU-R BS.2051 binaural rendering pipeline for multi-channel to stereo conversion; the interaural delay in the SOFA file processing for Head-Related Transfer Function playback; the ITD parameter used in the Max/MSP binaural panner object for interactive spatial audio [formal: differentia temporis interauralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: time-frequency-masking
payload.scope: A computational audio enhancement method that applies psychoacoustic masking thresholds across time-frequency bins to suppress noise and artifacts.

definition.body: Time-frequency-masking is a signal processing method that suppresses spectral components in a time-frequency representation based on psychoacoustic masking thresholds, computed from the spectral envelope and frequency selectivity of human hearing. The procedure: (1) compute a time-frequency representation (STFT spectrogram or filterbank output); (2) estimate the long-term spectral envelope or use a critical-band filterbank (e.g., Gammatone) to compute masking thresholds per bin; (3) apply a mask matrix — set each bin's magnitude to zero (hard masking) or scale it (soft masking) where it falls below the computed threshold; (4) optionally reconstruct the time-domain signal via inverse transform. The method leverages simultaneous masking (a loud tone masks nearby frequencies) and temporal masking (a loud event masks preceding/following frames). Used in speech enhancement, music denoising, and perceptual audio coding. Parameters: the STFT or filterbank configuration, the masking model (simultaneous, temporal, or combined), and the masking margin in dB. Persistence: implemented in speech enhancement libraries, perceptual coding standards, and audio processing toolkits. e.g.: the time-frequency mask used in the NVIDIA DeepFilterNet speech enhancement pipeline for real-time noise suppression; the masking matrix in the ISO/IEC 13818-7 advanced audio coding (AAC) encoder for perceptual quantization; the TF-domain mask applied in the HTK speech recognition frontend for reverberation mitigation [formal: latein | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: wavelet-packet
payload.scope: A tree-structured time-frequency analysis method that recursively decomposes both approximation and detail coefficients of a wavelet transform, enabling optimal basis selection for signal representation.

definition.body: Wavelet-packet is a signal decomposition method that extends the discrete wavelet transform (DWT) by decomposing not only the approximation subbands at each level but also the detail subbands, producing a full binary tree of frequency-localized components. The procedure: (1) start with a signal and compute the standard DWT; (2) at each node of the decomposition tree, apply the same filter pair to both the approximation and detail outputs, recursively expanding the tree; (3) the result is a set of 2^L leaf nodes, each representing a distinct frequency band. The optimal leaf selection problem — choosing the best subset of nodes for a given representation — is solved by a cost function such as Shannon entropy. Used in image compression, denoising, and feature extraction. Parameters: the wavelet type, the decomposition depth, and the optimal basis selection criterion. Persistence: implemented in PyWavelets (pywt.WaveletPacket), MATLAB Wavelet Toolbox (wpdec, wptree), and scikit-image. e.g.: pywt.WaveletPacket with db4 wavelet in PyWavelets for ECG signal denoising; wpdec function in the MATLAB Wavelet Toolbox for audio feature extraction; pywt.WaveletPacket object for vibration-based fault detection in rotating machinery [formal: packet-wavelet | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-decorrelation
payload.scope: A cepstral-domain procedure that removes statistical dependencies between adjacent cepstral coefficients for speech and audio feature extraction.

definition.body: Cepstral-decorrelation is a signal processing procedure that transforms cepstral coefficient vectors to remove statistical dependencies between coefficients, producing decorrelated representations that reduce redundancy. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstral coefficient vector c[n] of length N; (2) estimate the covariance matrix C of c[n] across a training set; (3) compute the Cholesky decomposition L such that C = LL^T; (4) transform each frame: c_d[n] = L^{-1} * c[n]. The result is a set of coefficients with near-zero cross-correlation. Used in speaker recognition, speech coding, and robust feature extraction. Parameters: the coefficient length N, the training set, and the regularization parameter. Persistence: implemented in speaker recognition toolkits and Python speech processing libraries. e.g.: cepstral decorrelation in Kaldi's x-vector speaker recognition pipeline; PCA decorrelation of MFCC features in NIST SRE 2018 evaluation; Cholesky decorrelation in LibriSpeech speaker verification baseline [formal: decomplexatio cepstrali | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-denoising
payload.scope: A cepstral-domain noise reduction method that separates speech cepstral components from noise by thresholding and filtering in the quefrency domain.

definition.body: Cepstral-denoising is a noise reduction method that operates in the cepstral (quefrency) domain, separating speech components from noise by exploiting their different quefrency structures. The procedure: (1) compute the cepstrum c[q] of a noisy speech frame via FFT, log-power spectrum, and inverse FFT; (2) identify speech-dominant quefrency ranges (typically quefrency > 1 ms for vocal tract, < 1 ms for pitch) and noise-dominant ranges; (3) apply quefrency-domain filtering: zero out or reduce coefficients in noise-dominant ranges, attenuate noise peaks; (4) inverse-transform the modified cepstrum to obtain the enhanced signal. Used in speech enhancement, audio restoration, and robust speech recognition. Parameters: the cepstrum type (real or complex), the quefrency thresholds for speech/noise separation, the filtering method (hard thresholding, soft thresholding, Wiener-like). Persistence: implemented in speech enhancement libraries and toolkits. e.g.: cepstral thresholding denoising in the HTK speech recognition frontend for noisy speech enhancement; the quefrency-domain Wiener filter used in the VoiceBox MATLAB toolkit for speech enhancement; cepstral domain filtering in the OpenSmile feature extraction system for noisy audio preprocessing [formal: deimpedimentatio cepstrali | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: A cepstral-domain technique for recovering fine spectral detail lost through smoothing or envelope extraction, using quefrency-domain processing.

definition.body: Cepstral-deresolution is a signal processing method that recovers high-resolution spectral detail suppressed by envelope-extraction or smoothing procedures, by inverting or compensating for quefrency-domain filtering. The procedure: (1) obtain the smoothed or envelope cepstrum c_env[q] via low-pass liftering; (2) obtain the full cepstrum c_full[q] of the original signal; (3) compute the residual: c_res[q] = c_full[q] - c_env[q], isolating fine spectral detail; (4) optionally enhance the residual via thresholding or normalization. The result is a detail component that, when added back to the envelope, reconstructs the full spectrum. Used in speech enhancement, source separation, and spectral recovery. Parameters: the lifter order (quefrency cutoff), the residual computation method, and the enhancement strategy. Persistence: implemented in speech processing research code and audio restoration toolkits. e.g.: the cepstral residual computed in the HTS-SPICE speech enhancement system for noise robustness; the quefrency-domain dereverberation using cepstral resolution in the ITU-T G.729 Annex Q standard; the cepstral detail component extracted in the NIST speaker recognition evaluation for fine speaker characterization [formal: resolucio cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-rate
payload.scope: People made cepstral-rate to measure how quickly cepstral coefficients change between consecutive frames of an audio signal, capturing temporal dynamics of spectral change.

definition.body: Cepstral-rate measures how quickly cepstral coefficients change between consecutive frames of an audio signal, capturing the temporal dynamics of spectral change. The procedure: (1) compute cepstral coefficients c[n] for consecutive frames n and n+1; (2) compute the first difference delta[n] = c[n+1] - c[n]; (3) compute the L2 norm of delta[n] as the cepstral-rate, optionally weighted by quefrency-dependent factors to emphasize perceptually relevant coefficients. Parameters: (1) the input signal frames, (2) the number of cepstral coefficients M, (3) the frame shift in samples, (4) optional quefrency weighting. Persistence: used in speech segmentation for detecting syllable and phoneme boundaries in Kaldi and HTK; in music information retrieval for onset detection; in speaker change detection in diarization pipelines. e.g.: the cepstral-rate feature used in Kaldi for syllable boundary detection in forced alignment; the spectral change rate computed in HTK for speech segmentation in the SPHERE evaluation; the first-difference cepstral magnitude used in NIST diarization for speaker change point detection | not: delta-cepstral-coefficients (per-coefficient differences, not the aggregate rate); cepstral-smoothing (averaging over frames, not measuring change) [formal: celeritas cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-extrapolation
payload.scope: People made cepstral-extrapolation to predict future cepstral coefficients beyond observed data using models of historical cepstral trajectories.

definition.body: Cepstral-extrapolation estimates future cepstral coefficients beyond the range of observed data, using models trained on historical cepstral sequences to predict continuation of spectral dynamics. The procedure: (1) compute a sequence of cepstral coefficients from observed frames; (2) fit a linear regression or autoregressive model to the cepstral trajectories; (3) extrapolate the model beyond the observed quefrency or frame range; (4) optionally inverse-transform the extrapolated cepstrum to obtain predicted spectral or time-domain signals. Parameters: (1) the observed cepstral sequence, (2) the extrapolation horizon (frames or quefrency steps), (3) the model order for trajectory prediction. Persistence: used in speech prediction for buffer management in real-time ASR systems; in audio synthesis for extending cepstral representations in HTS-HMM systems; in robust speech recognition for handling variable-length utterances. e.g.: the cepstral prediction module in Kaldi for lookahead buffer management in streaming ASR; the HTS-HMM cepstral trajectory extrapolation for speech synthesis continuation; the autoregressive cepstral prediction in Praat for voice conversion frame extension | not: cepstral-interpolation (estimating between observed points, not beyond them); cepstral-smoothing (averaging, not forward prediction) [formal: extrapolatio cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made cepstral-correlation to measure similarity of cepstral coefficient patterns across frames or between signals.

definition.body: Cepstral-correlation quantifies the similarity of cepstral coefficient patterns across frames or between signals, capturing temporal or cross-channel coherence of spectral structure. The procedure: (1) compute cepstral coefficients for two sequences or frames; (2) normalize each sequence to zero mean and unit variance; (3) compute the Pearson correlation coefficient between corresponding coefficient indices across the sequences. Parameters: (1) the two cepstral sequences to compare, (2) the number of coefficients M, (3) whether weighting is applied across quefrency indices. payload.scope: People made cepstral-coherence to measure the consistency of spectral structure across frames or channels.

definition.body: Cepstral-coherence measures the consistency of spectral structure across frames or between channels by computing the normalized similarity of cepstral coefficient patterns. The procedure: (1) compute cepstral coefficients for two or more frames or channel observations; (2) normalize each cepstral vector to zero mean and unit variance per coefficient index; (3) compute the coherence as the cosine similarity between the normalized vectors, yielding a value between -1 and 1 where 1 indicates identical spectral shape. Parameters: (1) the cepstral vectors to compare, (2) the number of coefficients M, (3) optional quefrency weighting to emphasize perceptually relevant coefficients. payload.scope: People made cepstral-slope to measure the rate of change of cepstral coefficients across coefficient indices, characterizing spectral tilt.

definition.body: Cepstral-slope measures the rate of change of cepstral coefficients across coefficient indices, characterizing the spectral tilt or high-frequency roll-off of a signal. The procedure: (1) compute cepstral coefficients c[0], c[1], ..., c[M-1]; (2) fit a linear regression model c[m] = a + b*m across the coefficient indices; (3) the cepstral-slope is the regression coefficient b, where negative values indicate high-frequency attenuation and positive values indicate spectral brightening. Parameters: (1) the cepstral coefficients, (2) the number of coefficients M, (3) the quefrency range over which to fit the regression. Persistence: used in speech recognition for spectral tilt normalization in Kaldi; in speaker recognition for voice quality analysis; in music information retrieval for timbre classification. e.g.: the cepstral-slope feature used in Kaldi for spectral tilt normalization in front-end processing; the cepstral-slope coefficient in HTK for speaker-dependent voice quality assessment; the linear cepstral regression slope in NIST speaker recognition evaluation for timbre classification [formal: declivitas cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Cepstral-trajectory represents the time-varying path of cepstral coefficients across consecutive frames of an audio signal, capturing how spectral shape evolves over time as a sequence of coefficient vectors. Parameters: (1) the input signal frames, (2) the number of cepstral coefficients M, (3) the frame rate in frames per second, (4) the trajectory model order. definition.body: Cepstral-silence-detection identifies silent or unvoiced segments in audio signals by analyzing the magnitude and distribution of cepstral coefficients, which approach near-zero values during silence. The procedure: (1) compute cepstral coefficients for consecutive frames; (2) evaluate silence criteria such as the total cepstral energy (sum of squared coefficients), the energy in the first coefficient c[0] representing signal power, or the variance of coefficients across the quefrency range; (3) classify frames as silent when metrics fall below adaptive or fixed thresholds. Parameters: (1) the input audio frames, (2) the number of cepstral coefficients M, (3) the silence threshold value, (4) the frame shift in samples. Persistence: used in speech recognition for VAD and silence trimming in Kaldi front-ends; in speaker diarization for silence segmentation in NIST evaluations; in audio processing for activity detection in HTK-based pipelines. e.g.: the cepstral-based VAD in Kaldi for automatic speech transcription silence trimming; the cepstral energy threshold in HTK for speaker diarization activity detection; the cepstral silence detection in Praat for automated speech annotation [formal: detectio silentii cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-drift
payload.scope: People made cepstral-drift to measure systematic shifts in cepstral statistics over time, capturing channel or environment changes.

definition.body: Cepstral-drift measures systematic shifts in cepstral coefficient statistics over time, capturing gradual changes in acoustic environment, channel characteristics, or speaker state. The procedure: (1) compute cepstral coefficients for consecutive frames or windows; (2) track the mean and variance of each coefficient index over a sliding window; (3) compute the drift as the temporal derivative of the coefficient means, or the Mahalanobis distance between current and reference coefficient distributions. Parameters: (1) the cepstral coefficient sequence, (2) the reference statistics for drift comparison, (3) the window size for tracking, (4) the drift threshold for alerting. Persistence: used in speech recognition for adaptive cepstral normalization in Kaldi online processing; in speaker recognition for session variability compensation in NIST evaluations; in audio surveillance for acoustic environment change detection in HTK-based pipelines. e.g.: the cepstral drift adaptation in Kaldi for online speaker adaptation in streaming ASR; the cepstral distribution shift detection in HTK for session variability normalization; the cepstral drift metric in Praat for monitoring recording environment changes [formal: devium cepstrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: wiener-filtering
payload.scope: People made it to optimally restore signals degraded by additive noise using spectral information about both the desired signal and the noise.

definition.body: Wiener-filtering is an optimal linear filtering procedure for signal restoration in the presence of additive noise, computed from the power spectral densities of the desired signal and the noise. The procedure: (1) compute the FFT of the noisy observation; (2) estimate the power spectral density of the clean signal S_dd(f) and the noise S_nn(f); (3) compute the Wiener gain W(f) = S_dd(f) / (S_dd(f) + S_nn(f)); (4) multiply the FFT by W(f); (5) inverse FFT to recover the filtered signal. When signal and noise are uncorrelated, the filter minimizes mean-square error. Parameters: the noisy input, the signal PSD estimate, the noise PSD estimate, and the block length for STFT-based processing. Persistence: implemented in speech enhancement systems, image denoising, seismic processing, and radar; documented in signal processing theory. e.g.: the spectral Wiener filter in the Babel speech enhancement system; MATLAB's wiener2 function for image denoising; the Wiener filter in the Lytro light-field camera for noise reduction; Proakis & Manolakis's Wiener filter algorithm for signal estimation | not: spectral-subtraction (subtracts noise PSD estimate instead of optimally weighting); cepstral-whitening (equalizes via quefrency-domain liftering, not PSD-based frequency weighting) [formal: filtrum wienense | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

definition.body: Log-power-spectrum is the base-10 logarithm of the power spectral density of a signal, computed from the squared magnitude of its Fourier transform. payload.name: power-spectrum-density
payload.scope: Computed to characterize how a signal's power is distributed across frequency, enabling spectral analysis, filter design, and noise estimation.

definition.body: Power-spectrum-density (PSD) quantifies how the power of a signal or time series is distributed as a function of frequency. The procedure: (1) compute the FFT X(f) of the signal (or its windowed segment for STFT); (2) compute the squared magnitude |X(f)| squared; (3) normalize by the sampling rate, the window energy, and the observation length to yield PSD in units of power per Hz. For random processes, PSD is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function (Wiener-Khinchin theorem). Parameters: the input signal, the window function and its normalization, the FFT length, and the overlap factor for Welch averaging. Persistence: computed in every spectral analysis pipeline (audio, communications, seismic); implemented in MATLAB's pwelch and periodogram functions, Python's scipy.signal.welch, NumPy's numpy.fft, and Praat's spectral analysis. e.g.: MATLAB's pwelch function using Welch's method for PSD estimation; Python's scipy.signal.welch for spectral density computation; the periodogram computed in NumPy's numpy.fft module; the PSD estimation in Praat for audio spectral analysis | not: power-spectrum (unnormalized spectral magnitude lacking the PSD's units of power-per-Hertz); log-power-spectrum (the logarithmic transform of PSD, not PSD itself) [formal: densitas spectrum potentiae | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

Parameters: the input signal, the FFT length, and any zero-padding or windowing applied before the transform. Persistence: the foundation for all inverse transforms (IFFT), phase vocoder processing, homomorphic filtering, and any application requiring phase coherence; implemented in the inverse FFT of NumPy, MATLAB's ifft, and the phase aware stages of Praat spectral analysis. e.g.: the inverse FFT in NumPy numpy.fft.ifft for reconstructing a signal from its complex coefficients; MATLAB ifft function for complex spectrum inversion; the complex FFT output in SciPy scipy.fft.fft used for phase aware processing; the complex spectrum computed in Praat for signal reconstruction | not: magnitude-spectrum (only the absolute value, lacking the phase information essential for reconstruction); log-power-spectrum (the log-magnitude only, lacking phase) [formal: spectrum complexum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: speaker-recognition
payload.scope: Built to identify or verify who is speaking by analyzing voice characteristics, enabling authentication, diarization, and speaker-dependent processing.

definition.body: Speaker-recognition is the process of identifying or verifying a speaker's identity from their vocal characteristics, independent of the linguistic content being spoken. The procedure: (1) extract voice features (typically MFCCs, PLPs, or x-vector embeddings) from speech segments; (2) match features against enrolled speaker models using distance metrics, classifiers (GMM-UBM, i-vector, d-vector), or neural network classifiers; (3) output a speaker identity or verification decision with confidence score. Two modes: identification (closed-set: which speaker among N candidates) and verification (open-set: is this speaker who they claim to be?). Parameters: the input audio, the feature extraction method, the speaker model, and the decision threshold for verification. Persistence: standardized in NIST Speaker Recognition Evaluations (SRE), implemented in Kaldi's speaker recognition toolkit, OpenSpeakerModel, and PyTorch-based speaker verification frameworks; used in voice authentication, forensic speech analysis, and call center applications. e.g.: the x-vector speaker recognition system used in the NIST SRE 2018 evaluation; Kaldi's idtools and xvector extraction for i-vector based speaker ID; the PyTorch Speaker Verification toolkit implementing angular margin loss for speaker embedding; OpenSpeakerModel's pre-trained d-vector models for speaker classification | not: speech-recognition (identifies what is said, not who is speaking); voice-activity-detection (determines if speech is present, not who speaks) [formal: recognitio locutoris | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-normalization
payload.scope: Designed to reduce channel distortion in speech features by normalizing cepstral coefficients across frames, improving robustness in speech and speaker processing.

definition.body: Cepstral-normalization is a feature normalization procedure that reduces channel and environmental distortion by standardizing cepstral coefficients across utterances or frames. The procedure: (1) compute cepstral coefficients (typically MFCCs) for all frames in a recording; (2) compute per-frequency-frame statistics (mean and optionally variance) across the utterance; (3) subtract the mean (CMN), and optionally divide by the standard deviation (CMVN). Parameters: the cepstral coefficient matrix, the normalization scope (per-utterance, per-session, or global), and whether variance normalization is applied. Persistence: implemented in Kaldi's cmvn and apply-cmvn tools, HTK's cepstral normalization, NIST speaker recognition pipelines, and Sphinx-4; used in every ASR and speaker recognition frontend for channel normalization. e.g.: Kaldi's featbin/cmvn for cepstral mean and variance normalization; HTK's cepstral normalization applied before GMM training; NIST SRE pipelines using utterance-level CMVN for x-vector extraction; Sphinx-4's cepstral normalization for real-time recognition | not: cepstral-whitening (quefrency-domain envelope equalization, not frame-wise statistics); cepstral-smoothing (low-pass filtering in quefrency, not statistical standardization) [formal: normalizatio cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: phase-reconstruction
payload.scope: Needed to recover phase information lost during processing or transmission, enabling signal reconstruction from magnitude-only representations.

definition.body: Phase-reconstruction is the computational process of recovering the phase spectrum of a signal from incomplete or lost phase information, typically using iterative algorithms or learned priors. The procedure: (1) obtain the magnitude spectrum (or a magnitude-only representation); (2) initialize phase estimates (random or from a heuristic); (3) iterate between time-domain and frequency-domain constraints until convergence; (4) apply the reconstructed phase to the magnitude spectrum and inverse transform to recover the signal. Persistence: implemented in Griffin-Lim algorithm for speech synthesis, deep learning approaches like DCCRN for phase reconstruction, and audio restoration pipelines; used in speech synthesis, audio source separation, and audio enhancement. e.g.: the Griffin-Lim algorithm used in early speech synthesis systems for phase recovery from mel-spectrograms; DCCRN deep learning model for end-to-end speech enhancement with phase reconstruction; Wave-U-Net for audio source separation with learned phase priors; PhaseCon learned phase reconstruction for musical audio | not: complex-spectrum (has phase inherently, no reconstruction needed); magnitude-spectrum (lacks phase, not the reconstruction process) [formal: reconstructio phasei | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: x-vector
payload.scope: Created to produce fixed-length speaker embeddings from variable-length speech for robust speaker recognition and verification.

definition.body: X-vector is a speaker embedding representation that encodes variable-length speech into a fixed-dimensional vector capturing speaker identity, produced by a time-delay neural network (TDNN) with statistics pooling. The procedure: (1) compute frame-level features (e.g. MFCCs or filterbank features); (2) pass through a TDNN to extract frame-level representations; (3) apply statistics pooling (frame mean and standard deviation) to produce a fixed-length segment-level representation; (4) pass through a classifier layer to produce the final embedding vector. Parameters: the feature extraction method, the TDNN architecture depth and frame context, the embedding dimension (typically 512), and the training loss (e.g. AAM softmax). Persistence: standardized in the NIST SRE 2018 evaluation as the primary speaker embedding; implemented in Kaldi's xvector tools, PyTorch Speaker Verification toolkit, and OpenSpeakerModel; used in speaker diarization, verification, and identification systems. e.g.: the x-vector system in Kaldi's xvector/ directory for NIST SRE 2018; the PyTorch Speaker Verification toolkit's x-vector model training; OpenSpeakerModel's pretrained x-vector embeddings for speaker classification; the x-vector diarization system used in NIST Rich Translation Evaluation | not: i-vector (GMM-based speaker embedding using total variability space, not neural statistics pooling); cepstral-coefficients (raw acoustic features, not speaker embeddings) [formal: vector x | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-noise-estimation
payload.scope: A noise estimation procedure that tracks noise cepstral statistics during voiceless segments to produce a noise profile for subsequent cepstral-domain noise suppression.

definition.body: Cepstral-noise-estimation is a procedure that computes statistical estimates of noise cepstral coefficients from voiceless or silent segments of a speech signal, producing a noise profile used in subsequent cepstral-domain noise subtraction or suppression. The procedure: (1) detect speech activity (using VAD or energy-based thresholds); (2) collect cepstral coefficients from detected noise-only segments; (3) accumulate statistics (running average, minimum statistics, or recursive update) across these segments; (4) produce a smoothed noise cepstrum estimate. Parameters: (1) the voice activity detection method, (2) the accumulation strategy (initial segments, minimum statistics, recursive exponential averaging), (3) the update rate for non-stationary noise. Persistence: documented in speech enhancement literature, implemented in Kaldi's cmvn and VAD tools for noise-aware normalization, HTK's noise estimation utilities, and commercial ASR frontend pipelines for robust recognition in noisy conditions. e.g.: minimum statistics noise tracking in the MATLAB speech enhancement toolbox; Kaldi's VAD-gated cepstral mean computation for adaptive normalization; HTK's initial segment noise estimation for HMM training; the recursive noise update in the WebRTC noise suppressor's cepstral statistics | not: cepstral-subtraction (subtracts the estimated noise, does not estimate it); cepstral-whitening (equalizes spectral envelope, does not estimate noise) [formal: aestimatio noise cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-noise-suppression
payload.scope: A speech enhancement technique that reduces additive noise by applying a suppression gain computed from noise cepstral estimates in the quefrency domain.

definition.body: Cepstral-noise-suppression is a speech enhancement technique that reduces additive noise by computing a suppression gain in the cepstral domain and applying it to the noisy speech cepstrum before inverse transformation. The procedure: (1) estimate noise cepstral coefficients from noise-only segments; (2) compute a suppression gain as a function of the ratio between noisy and noise-only cepstral power; (3) apply the gain to the noisy cepstrum to attenuate noise-dominated quefrency components; (4) inverse-transform to recover the enhanced speech spectrum. Parameters: (1) the noise estimation method (initial segments, minimum statistics, recursive), (2) the gain function form (spectral subtraction, Wiener filter, MMSE), (3) spectral floor to prevent musical noise. Persistence: documented in the speech enhancement literature, implemented in Praat's noise reduction tools, MATLAB's Speech Recognition Toolbox for noise robustness, and custom Python/C++ pipelines for ASR frontends in noisy environments. e.g.: spectral subtraction noise suppression in the MATLAB Speech Recognition Toolbox; Praat's spectral subtraction for speech enhancement; the spectral subtraction algorithm in OpenSMILE's noise robustness feature extraction; the Wiener filter cepstral suppression in custom Python ASR frontends | not: cepstral-noise-estimation (estimates noise statistics, does not suppress); cepstral-subtraction (operates by direct subtraction of noise cepstrum, not by gain computation) [formal: suppressio noise cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-spectral-subtraction
payload.scope: A noise reduction technique that combines cepstral-domain noise estimation with spectral-domain subtraction, computing a gain function from noise statistics in the cepstral domain.

definition.body: Cepstral-spectral-subtraction is a speech enhancement technique that combines cepstral-domain noise estimation with spectral-domain gain application. The procedure: (1) compute the short-time Fourier transform of the noisy speech frame; (2) estimate the noise spectral magnitude from noise-only cepstral statistics; (3) compute a spectral subtraction gain as the ratio of noisy to estimated noise power; (4) apply the gain to the noisy spectral magnitude; (5) apply phase from the noisy signal for reconstruction. Parameters: (1) the noise estimation strategy, (2) the spectral floor to prevent musical noise, (3) the over-subtraction factor. Persistence: documented in the speech enhancement literature, implemented in the MATLAB speech enhancement toolbox for noise reduction, Praat's noise suppression module, the WebRTC noise suppressor's spectral processing pipeline, and Python speech processing libraries for ASR frontend enhancement. e.g.: the spectral subtraction algorithm in the MATLAB Speech Recognition Toolbox; Praat's noise reduction using spectral subtraction; the WebRTC noise suppressor's spectral processing; the spectral subtraction implementation in the Python SpeechPy library | not: cepstral-noise-estimation (estimates noise, does not apply spectral gain); cepstral-subtraction (subtracts noise cepstrum directly, not in spectral domain) [formal: subtrahium spectrale cepstrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cepstral-spectral-floor
payload.scope: A spectral floor parameter that prevents negative values and musical noise when subtracting noise estimates in the cepstral or spectral domain.

definition.body: Cepstral-spectral-floor is a floor parameter applied to noise-estimated spectral or cepstral values to prevent negative results and suppress musical noise artifacts that arise from over-subtraction. The procedure: (1) estimate noise cepstral or spectral coefficients; (2) compute the subtraction or gain; (3) clamp the result to a minimum floor value; (4) the floor level is typically set as a fraction of the noise estimate (e.g., alpha times the noise spectral magnitude). Parameters: (1) the floor level (absolute dB, or a fraction like 0.01 of the noise estimate), (2) whether applied in spectral or cepstral domain, (3) the over-subtraction factor that the floor compensates. Persistence: documented in speech enhancement literature, implemented as the spectral floor parameter in the MATLAB Speech Recognition Toolbox, the minNoiseFloor in WebRTC noise suppressor, Praat's noise floor control, and the spectral floor in the Kaldi speech processing toolkit's noise reduction components. e.g.: the spectral floor parameter in MATLAB's Speech Recognition Toolbox noise reduction; WebRTC noise suppressor's minNoiseFloor constant; Praat's spectral floor control in the noise reduction module; the spectral floor in Kaldi's noise robustness feature extraction pipeline | not: cepstral-noise-estimation (produces noise estimate, not a floor); cepstral-subtraction (the subtraction operation itself, not the floor clamping) [formal: floor spectrale cepstrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]
